findings.element: The measure on a plan built through the real first-run path (state=owner-empty, set the day, add a moment) — .b-measure
findings.problem: Driven end to end, a brand-new owner's plan has no end. Set 3 October, add one moment, and the measure renders 'Today, 16 July', a single row at 40 days, and then roughly 700px of bare rule running down into the dark with nothing at the bottom of it. The day the whole page is measured from — the only thing the owner has actually entered, the thing the 96px count above it is counting — is not on the measure at all. The seeded demo hides this because its fixture happens to carry 'Wedding day' as a milestone; the state a real first user reaches is a line into nothing, which is the exact opposite of the direction's claim that everything approaches a horizon. This is the first plan any founder or customer will ever build, and it is the one plan where the composition's central idea does not resolve.
findings.fix: In render-b.js, derive the measure's terminus from F.project.primaryDate rather than from a milestone. After placing F.milestones, always append one terminus row positioned at days(F.today, F.project.primaryDate.date), carrying the primaryDate label and its formatted date, drawn with the same full-width hairline, hollow tick and 600 weight the seeded plan's last row already gets, and excluded from the moment count and from the 'Behind you' record so no count changes. Every plan's measure then ends on the day, seeded or built.

findings.element: The last item on the measure — .b-item (day) .b-title — phone, desk and print
findings.problem: The composition is a distance, so the scroll is the approach; but what the approach arrives at is 17px/600 on a phone and 24px/600 at desk — the same size as 'Final dress fitting' and 'Choose the evening music', separated from an errand only by weight. On a phone that means about 1700px of travel that lands on a slightly bolder line of body type. The row is correctly MARKED (hairline across the measure, one filled tick reserved elsewhere) but it is not FELT: the page spends 96px on how far away the day is and eleven point sizes less on the day itself when you finally reach it. This is not the arrival-animation request refuted twice — it asks for no motion at all; position stays the quantity and nothing moves.
findings.fix: Give the terminus its own step on the existing ramp. Add a rule for the day row's title: 24/600 below 701px and 30/600 at 701px and above (both are declared ramp steps), leading --lead-title, its date line held at 12 mono as now; keep the count column, the hairline and the hollow tick exactly as they are so the 96px horizon count remains the largest thing in the composition. Apply the same step to the printed sheet's last row.

findings.element: state=owner-draft, its own Publish button, and the press headline h1.b-pressTitle it lands on
findings.problem: The fourteenth state paints the draft branch correctly — 'A plan nobody holds yet', 'Only you can see this', today's stamp — but states["owner-draft"] restores F.publication to the seeded published record on the same tick it renders. So pressing that screen's own Publish lands on the published branch: a 48px headline reading 'Mara & Finn have had this since 15 July', one day before the stamp on the screen the owner just pressed from, and returning to the plan then says 'Live since 15 July'. The sentence that branch was written for — 'Send it to Mara & Finn.' — exists in the file and never paints on this route; I reached it only by building a plan from the empty state. This is the emotional apex of the owner's whole journey, the state's own kicker is 'the moment it becomes theirs', and what it actually says is a provable falsehood about a handover that happened two seconds ago.
findings.fix: In render-b.js states["owner-draft"], commit the draft record instead of borrowing it: set F.publication = { state: "draft", publishedAt: null } and F.updatedLabel to today's medium date, render the surface, and delete the two restoring assignments (F.publication = was; F.updatedLabel = wasLabel). Restore the seeded record where owner-empty already does it — on entry to any state that is not this project — so the draft branch survives the navigation that leaves it.

findings.element: The received artifact's foot on a phone, below the 'Behind you' fold
findings.problem: The owner's chain ends in something to keep: an A4 keepsake that is the best object in the system. The audience's chain ends in a full stop. Driven cold on a phone, the whole received artifact offers a guest exactly one control — the 'Behind you' fold — and no way to take the day with them; they close the tab holding nothing, and the next thing Signal Timeline ever says to them is 'This link has ended.' For the flagship case that is a wedding guest, a mother, a venue, the one thing they will actually want from the screen is the date in their own calendar, and the artifact treats that want as though it does not exist. The page reads as something to admire rather than something that enters your life.
findings.fix: Add one control to the received foot, under the fold, in the mono label register at 44px, no new tokens: 'Keep the day'. It writes a single-event .ics built from data already on the page — all-day event on F.project.primaryDate, title the project name and the day's label, the share URL in the description — and nothing else. State the scope once, in words, in the 13px line beneath it: 'Adds Saturday 3 October to your calendar. Nothing else is shared.' Print keeps it as the typed date it already has; the ended state does not render it.

biggestWin: The morning. Open state=day cold on a phone and it is the one screen in the system that moves you: the name in 12px mono, then 'Today' set at 96/600 and centred — the only centred composition in the product, so the change of register alone tells you the counting has stopped — 'Saturday 3 October 2026' under it, a hairline, and then one quiet sentence, 'This is the day the plan was for.' Nothing counts down, nothing asks for anything, and the past folds itself into a single line. That is the memorable moment, and it is real: a stranger would believe a top studio made it and would forward it. Two things sit between it and a 9.5. First, it is the only one — the approach that leads to it has no payoff of its own, so the emotion is all in the last screen rather than in the journey the direction is named for. Second, everything before it is craft of a very high order rather than feeling: the empty state's single question ('When is the day?'), the printed keepsake, the stalled load that says nothing was deleted. What remains is small in engineering terms and not small in effect: two of my four findings are polish measured in type steps and one line of state handling, one is a genuine build (something the guest can keep), and none of them asks to reopen the lock.
